claim: Overflow metabolism refers to the production of seemingly wasteful by-products by cells during growth on glucose even when oxygen is abundant.
source: Overflow metabolism refers to the production of seemingly wasteful by-products by cells during growth on glucose even when oxygen is abundant.
evidence: This is a definitional statement that establishes the concept being studied in the manuscript.

claim: Yeasts produce ethanol as overflow metabolism, a phenomenon known as the Crabtree effect.
source: yeasts produce ethanol (a phenomenon known as the Crabtree effect; Crabtree, 1929)
evidence: Supported by citation to Crabtree, 1929.

claim: Mammalian cells produce lactate as overflow metabolism, known as the Warburg effect in cancer cells.
source: mammalian cells produce lactate (the Warburg effect in cancer cells; Warburg, 1956)
evidence: Supported by citation to Warburg, 1956.

claim: Bacteria produce small organic acids such as acetate as overflow metabolism.
source: bacteria produce small organic acids such as acetate (Harden, 1901)
evidence: Supported by citation to Harden, 1901.

claim: Acetate production in E. coli results from an imbalance between the bacterium's capacities to produce and assimilate acetyl-CoA.
source: Acetate production is considered to result from an imbalance between E. coli's capacities to produce and assimilate acetyl-CoA, the main precursor of acetate.
evidence: This represents established understanding in the field based on stoichiometric models.

claim: Stoichiometric models suggest that the imbalance causing acetate overflow could be caused by various cell-level constraints including energy conservation, recycling of cofactors, membrane occupancy, and resource allocation.
source: Stoichiometric models suggest that this imbalance could be caused by various cell-level constraints, such as energy conservation (de Groot et al., 2020; El-Mansi and Holms, 1989), recycling of cofactors (Wolfe, 2005; Vemuri et al., 2006), membrane occupancy (Zhuang et al., 2011; Szenk et al., 2017), and resource allocation (Basan et al., 2015; Zeng and Yang, 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published models.

claim: Stoichiometric models successfully predict the growth rate dependence of acetate production in E. coli.
source: These models – and the underlying theories – capture the essence of the overflow process and successfully predict the growth rate dependence of acetate production in E. coli (Basan et al., 2015; Zeng and Yang, 2019; Renilla et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Increases in extracellular acetate concentration can interrupt or even reverse the acetate flux in E. coli.
source: However, none of these theories explain why increases in extracellular acetate concentration can interrupt or even reverse the acetate flux in E. coli (Enjalbert et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Enjalbert et al., 2017.

claim: E. coli is able to co-consume glucose and acetate even when glucose is abundant.
source: which is able to co-consume glucose and acetate even when glucose is abundant
evidence: This is stated as an established observation in the manuscript.

claim: Cell growth is not affected when acetate production is abolished in E. coli.
source: Cell growth is not affected when acetate production is abolished (Enjalbert et al., 2017; Lee and Liao, 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Enjalbert et al., 2017 and Lee and Liao, 2008.

claim: Acetate overflow is neither necessary for E. coli to sustain fast growth nor strictly imposed by proposed constraints.
source: suggesting that this overflow is neither necessary for E. coli to sustain fast growth nor strictly imposed by the proposed constraints
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that growth is not affected when acetate production is abolished.

claim: A kinetic model of the Pta-AckA pathway has successfully been used to predict the reversal of the acetate flux at high acetate concentrations.
source: For example, a kinetic model of the Pta-AckA pathway has successfully been used to predict the reversal of the acetate flux at high acetate concentrations (Enjalbert et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Enjalbert et al., 2017.

claim: The reversal of acetate flux at high acetate concentrations is caused by thermodynamic control of the acetate pathway by the concentration of acetate itself.
source: This effect is caused by thermodynamic control of the acetate pathway by the concentration of acetate itself, a mechanism that operates independently of enzyme expression.
evidence: This is stated as an established finding from previous kinetic modeling work.

claim: The kinetic model includes three processes: glucose transport and conversion into acetyl-CoA, utilisation of acetyl-CoA in the TCA cycle and anabolic pathways for growth, and acetate metabolism.
source: This model includes three processes: (i) glucose transport and its conversion into acetyl-CoA by the glycolytic pathway, (ii) utilisation of acetyl-CoA in the TCA cycle (energy conservation) and anabolic pathways (production of building blocks) for growth, and (iii) acetate metabolism, i.e., the reversible conversion of acetyl-CoA into acetate via phosphotransacetylase (Pta), acetate kinase (AckA), and an acetate exchange reaction between the cell and its environment.
evidence: This describes the structure of the model constructed in this study.

claim: The initial model included two compartments, 6 species, 6 reactions, and 24 parameters.
source: This initial model included two compartments, 6 species, 6 reactions, and 24 parameters.
evidence: This describes the technical specifications of the model.

claim: The value of 14 parameters were taken directly from the literature.
source: The value of 14 parameters were taken directly from the literature (Enjalbert et al., 2017; Millard et al., 2017; Kadir et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature sources.

claim: Three growth experiments were performed on 13C-glucose (15 mM) plus different concentrations of 12C-acetate (1, 10, and 30 mM) to estimate remaining parameters.
source: To estimate the remaining parameters, we performed three growth experiments on 13C-glucose (15 mM) plus different concentrations of 12C-acetate (1, 10, and 30 mM), as detailed in Enjalbert et al., 2017.
evidence: This describes the experimental design used for parameter estimation.

claim: The initial model (model 1) without inhibition by acetate did not fit the data satisfactorily.
source: This initial model (model 1) did not fit the data satisfactorily (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1B and supplementary figures.

claim: Adding inhibition of the glycolytic pathway by acetate (model 2) improved the fits of biomass, glucose, and acetate concentration profiles but not of the acetate labelling profiles.
source: Adding inhibition of the glycolytic pathway by acetate (model 2) to account for the reduction in glucose uptake at high acetate concentrations improved the fits of the biomass, glucose, and acetate concentration profiles but not of the acetate labelling profiles (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by model fitting results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Adding inhibition of the TCA cycle by acetate (model 3) slightly improved the fit of the acetate labelling profile but not of the glucose and biomass concentration profiles.
source: Similarly, adding inhibition of the TCA cycle by acetate (model 3) slightly improved the fit of the acetate labelling profile but not of the glucose and biomass concentration profiles (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by model fitting results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: A sufficiently accurate fit was only achieved when both glycolysis and TCA cycle pathways were inhibited by acetate (model 4).
source: A sufficiently accurate fit was only achieved when both pathways were inhibited (model 4; Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by model fitting results shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: The model modifications suggest the existence of an unknown regulatory program that makes E. coli sensitive and responsive to acetate concentration.
source: These modifications suggest the existence of an unknown regulatory program that makes E. coli sensitive and responsive to acetate concentration
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results.

claim: The model modifications provide a mechanistic rationale for the reported 'toxicity' of acetate to E. coli.
source: and provide a mechanistic rationale for the reported 'toxicity' of acetate to E. coli (Enjalbert et al., 2017; Wilbanks and Trinh, 2017; Luli and Strohl, 1990; Pinhal et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to studies reporting acetate toxicity.

claim: Transcriptomic results revealed a global and progressive remodelling of gene expression at increasing acetate concentrations.
source: Transcriptomic results revealed a global and progressive remodelling of gene expression at increasing acetate concentrations (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The presence of acetate modulates the expression of genes involved in motility, biofilm formation, translation, stress response, metabolism, and transport of carbohydrates, amino acids, and ions.
source: We noted that the presence of acetate modulates the expression of genes involved in various biological functions: motility, biofilm formation, translation, stress response, metabolism, transport of carbohydrates, amino acids, and ions (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic data and Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The observed changes in gene expression cannot result solely from the inhibition of growth by acetate.
source: Importantly, the observed changes in gene expression cannot result solely from the inhibition of growth by acetate, as shown by comparing gene expression levels on glucose plus 100 mM acetate with those on glucose alone at the same growth rate (0.35 hr−1) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by comparison of gene expression data at matched growth rates shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Acetate reduces the expression of all genes that code for the glucose phosphotransferase system (PTS).
source: At the level of the central metabolism (Figure 2D), acetate reduces the expression of all genes that code for the glucose phosphotransferase system (PTS) (ptsGHI, crr)
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Acetate does not induce the expression of alternative systems of glucose internalisation and phosphorylation that could compensate for reduced PTS activity.
source: without inducing the expression of alternative systems of glucose internalisation and phosphorylation (galP, mglABC, glf, glk, manXYZ) that could have compensated for reduced PTS activity and the corresponding inhibition of glucose uptake (Lim and Jung, 2017; Ruyter et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic data and citations to studies on alternative glucose uptake systems.

claim: Expression of upper glycolytic genes remained stable, with the exception of fbaB and pfkB which were overexpressed in the presence of acetate.
source: Expression of upper glycolytic genes remained stable, with the exception of two isoenzymes that were overexpressed in the presence of acetate: fbaB, a gluconeogenic enzyme, and pfkB, which contributes little to phosphofructokinase activity on glucose (<10%) (Fraenkel, 1986; Scamuffa and Caprioli, 1980; Long and Antoniewicz, 2019; Daldal et al., 1982).
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic data and citations to studies on enzyme function.

claim: The expression of most lower glycolysis genes was reduced by 15–40% at 100 mM acetate.
source: In contrast, the expression of most of the lower glycolysis genes (pgk, gapA, gpmA, eno, pykF, aceE) was reduced by 15–40% at 100 mM acetate.
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic data.

claim: At 100 mM acetate, acetate inhibits the expression of virtually all TCA cycle genes by 30–67%.
source: At this concentration, acetate also inhibits the expression of virtually all TCA cycle genes (gltA, acnAB, icd, lpd, sucABCD, sdhABCD, fumABC, mdh) by 30–67%.
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic data.

claim: The expression of pta and ackA remained remarkably stable at all acetate concentrations.
source: In terms of acetate metabolism, the expression of pta and ackA, which code for enzymes in the Pta-AckA pathway, remained remarkably stable at all acetate concentrations.
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic data.

claim: Expression of pyruvate oxidase (poxB) was increased by a factor of 8 in the presence of acetate.
source: Expression of pyruvate oxidase (poxB) was increased by a factor of 8 in the presence of acetate
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic data.

claim: Pyruvate oxidase contributes to acetate metabolism mainly in the stationary phase and apparently not under the experimental conditions used.
source: though this promiscuous enzyme contributes to acetate metabolism mainly in the stationary phase and apparently not under our conditions (Enjalbert et al., 2017; Pinhal et al., 2019; Martínez-Gómez et al., 2012; Dittrich et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on pyruvate oxidase function.

claim: Expression of acetyl-CoA synthetase (acs) decreased with increasing acetate concentration.
source: Expression of acetyl-CoA synthetase (acs) – which converts acetate to acetyl-CoA with a high affinity – decreased with increasing acetate concentration
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic data.

claim: Under glucose excess, the presence of acetate does not activate acetate recycling through the Pta-AckA-Acs cycle.
source: indicating that under glucose excess, the presence of acetate does not activate acetate recycling through the Pta-AckA-Acs cycle (Enjalbert et al., 2017; Valgepea et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference from the transcriptomic data supported by citations.

claim: Acetate gradually modulates both the flux capacity of E. coli to produce acetyl-CoA from glucose and its capacity to utilise acetyl-CoA as a source of energy and anabolic precursors for growth.
source: These data confirm our hypothesis that acetate gradually modulates both the flux capacity of E. coli to produce acetyl-CoA from glucose and its capacity to utilise acetyl-CoA as a source of energy and of anabolic precursors for growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transcriptomic data.

claim: Acetate does not appear to influence the flux capacity of the acetate pathway itself.
source: Acetate does not appear to influence the flux capacity of the acetate pathway itself, which is also consistent with the proposed model.
evidence: This is an inference from the transcriptomic data showing stable pta and ackA expression.

claim: The model accurately reproduces the steady-state glucose and acetate fluxes in glucose-limited chemostat cultures at dilution rates of 0.1–0.5 hr−1.
source: The simulated profiles of acetate production as a function of growth and glucose uptake rates were in excellent agreement with experimental data (Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The model accurately predicts the growth and glucose uptake rates decrease monotonously with increasing acetate concentrations.
source: The growth and glucose uptake rates decreased monotonously with increasing acetate concentrations, in agreement with the experimental data (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The model predicts a progressive decrease of acetate production with increasing acetate concentration, and a reversal of the acetate flux above a threshold concentration of about 10 mM.
source: The acetate flux profile was also well described by the model, with a progressive decrease of acetate production with increasing acetate concentration, and a reversal of the acetate flux above a threshold concentration of about 10 mM.
evidence: Supported by model predictions compared to experimental data.

claim: The growth rate was not affected when acetate production was abolished, confirming that acetate production is not required to maintain fast growth.
source: As observed experimentally, the growth rate was not affected when acetate production was abolished, confirming that acetate production is not required to maintain fast growth nor is it imposed by any intracellular constraint.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from both model predictions and experimental data.

claim: The model accurately reproduces the rapid reversal of the acetate flux and reduction of glucose uptake after an acetate pulse.
source: Here again, the model accurately reproduces the experimental profiles, in particular the rapid reversal of the acetate flux and reduction of glucose uptake after the acetate pulse (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The model accurately predicts the steady-state and dynamic relationships between glucose uptake, growth, and acetate fluxes in E. coli over a broad range of glucose and acetate concentrations.
source: Overall, the predictions of the model are in agreement with experimental findings. The model accurately predicts the steady-state and dynamic relationships between glucose uptake, growth, and acetate fluxes in E. coli over a broad range of glucose and acetate concentrations.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the validation experiments.

claim: The most accurate predictions for all perturbations are those from the model with dual inhibition (model 4).
source: The most accurate predictions for all perturbations are those from the model with dual inhibition (model 4), followed by those from the single-inhibition models (models 2 and 3) and finally those produced by the no-inhibition model (model 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of variance-weighted sum of squared residuals shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The regulatory role of acetate in E. coli is functionally important.
source: The predicted data are thus only qualitatively and quantitatively consistent with observations when inhibition by acetate is included, indicating that the regulatory role of acetate in E. coli is functionally important.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model comparison analysis.

claim: Acetate flux is controlled to a similar degree by the acetate pathway (flux control coefficient of 0.76), glycolysis (0.88), and the TCA cycle (−0.64).
source: Metabolic control analysis revealed that rather than being controlled entirely from within the acetate pathway, acetate flux is controlled to a similar degree by the acetate pathway (with a flux control coefficient of 0.76), glycolysis (0.88), and the TCA cycle (−0.64).
evidence: Supported by metabolic control analysis calculations from the model.

claim: The balance between acetyl-CoA production and demand has a strong effect on acetate production.
source: The balance between acetyl-CoA production and demand (i.e., between glycolytic and TCA fluxes), therefore has a strong effect on acetate production.
evidence: This is an inference from the metabolic control analysis results.

claim: Acetate flux control is distributed around the acetyl-CoA node.
source: Overall, acetate flux control is distributed around the acetyl-CoA node.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the metabolic control analysis.

claim: The control exerted by the acetate pathway on acetate flux decreases non-linearly as the acetate concentration increases.
source: The control exerted by the acetate pathway on acetate flux decreases non-linearly as the acetate concentration increases (Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by metabolic control analysis results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There is a progressive shift of control from inside to outside the acetate pathway as acetate concentration increases.
source: highlighting a progressive shift of the control from inside to outside the acetate pathway
evidence: This is an interpretation of the control analysis results.

claim: Discontinuous control patterns are observed for glycolytic and TCA pathways at a concentration of about 10 mM, around the concentration threshold at which the acetate flux switches from production to consumption.
source: Discontinuous control patterns are observed for the latter pathways at a concentration of about 10 mM, i.e., around the concentration threshold at which the acetate flux switches from production to consumption and is zero (Enjalbert et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by metabolic control analysis results and citation to previous work.

claim: The sum of the control coefficients of the glycolytic and TCA blocks increases with the acetate concentration and compensates for the decrease in control from the acetate pathway.
source: The sum of the control coefficients of the glycolytic and TCA blocks, which represent the overall control exerted by E. coli metabolism on the acetate flux (Figure 5D), increases with the acetate concentration and compensates for the decrease in control from the acetate pathway.
evidence: Supported by metabolic control analysis results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Control shifts from the glycolytic pathway to the TCA cycle as the acetate concentration increases.
source: The ratio of the control coefficients of glycolysis and the TCA cycle show that control shifts from the glycolytic pathway to the TCA cycle as the acetate concentration increases (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by metabolic control analysis results shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The progressive transfer of control from the acetate pathway to the rest of the metabolism as a function of the acetate concentration emerges specifically from the inhibition by acetate of both the glycolytic and the TCA cycle pathways.
source: In models 1–3, the control exerted by the acetate pathway remains constant at low to moderate acetate concentrations and tends to increase at high acetate concentrations, indicating that the progressive transfer of control from the acetate pathway to the rest of the metabolism as a function of the acetate concentration emerges specifically from the inhibition by acetate of both the glycolytic and the TCA cycle pathways.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing control analysis results across different model versions.

claim: At low acetate concentrations (<10 mM), the main regulatory route (50–60%) is direct metabolic regulation via the acetate pathway, with the remaining flux response accounted for by indirect regulation through the TCA cycle (35–40%) and glycolysis (5–10%).
source: At low acetate concentrations (<10 mM), the main regulatory route (50–60%) is direct metabolic regulation via the acetate pathway, with the remaining flux response being accounted for by indirect regulation through the TCA cycle (35–40%) and glycolysis (5–10%).
evidence: Supported by partitioned response coefficient analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Above 10 mM acetate, direct regulation by acetate accounts for about 40% of the observed flux response, glycolysis about 20%, and the TCA cycle roughly 40%.
source: Above this threshold, direct regulation by acetate accounts for about 40% of the observed flux response, glycolysis, about 20%, and the TCA cycle, roughly 40%.
evidence: Supported by partitioned response coefficient analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: There are two distinct modes of regulation that depend on the acetate concentration and remain remarkably stable over a broad range of concentrations.
source: revealing two distinct modes of regulation that depend on the acetate concentration and remain remarkably stable over a broad range of concentrations
evidence: This is a conclusion from the response coefficient analysis.

claim: The kinetic model links acetate metabolism with glucose uptake and growth.
source: The kinetic model of E. coli metabolism developed in this work links acetate metabolism with glucose uptake and growth.
evidence: This describes the scope of the model developed.

claim: The model suggested the existence of a global regulatory program whereby the extracellular concentration of acetate determines the flux capacity of the glycolytic and TCA pathways.
source: This model suggested the existence of a global regulatory program whereby the extracellular concentration of acetate determines the flux capacity of the glycolytic and TCA pathways
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results.

claim: Inhibition of glycolytic and TCA pathways by acetate was required to explain the dynamic profiles obtained in 13C-labelling experiments.
source: whose inhibition was required to explain the dynamic profiles obtained in 13C-labelling experiments
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model fitting analysis.

claim: Inhibition of glycolytic and TCA pathways by acetate was necessary and sufficient to predict the steady-state and dynamic responses of E. coli to a broad range of perturbations.
source: This inhibition was also necessary (and sufficient) to predict the steady-state and dynamic responses of E. coli to a broad range of perturbations.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model validation analysis.

claim: Acetate regulates the flux capacity of glycolytic and TCA pathways at the transcriptional level by modulating the expression of most of their genes.
source: Transcriptomics experiments confirmed that acetate regulates the flux capacity of these two pathways at the transcriptional level by modulating the expression of most of their genes.
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Adjusting fluxes through transcriptional regulation is a highly efficient way for cells to maintain metabolite homeostasis.
source: This is a highly efficient way for cells to adjust their fluxes while maintaining metabolite homeostasis (Kacser and Burns, 1973; Heinrich and Rapoport, 1974).
evidence: Supported by citations to foundational metabolic control theory papers.

claim: The metabolic response of E. coli to changes in acetate concentration involves a global reorganisation of its metabolism from the transcriptional to the flux levels.
source: The metabolic response of E. coli to changes in acetate concentration thus involves a global reorganisation of its metabolism from the transcriptional to the flux levels
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined modeling and transcriptomic results.

claim: The coordinated regulation of the glycolytic and TCA pathways cannot be explained by the actions of known transcriptional regulators.
source: The coordinated regulation of the glycolytic and TCA pathways cannot be explained by the actions of known transcriptional regulators, suggesting that these regulators act in concert or that there are additional regulators present.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that the regulatory pattern doesn't match known regulators.

claim: Transcriptional regulation occurs in a few minutes, which is sufficiently fast to explain most observations.
source: Transcriptional regulation occurs in a few minutes (Enjalbert et al., 2013; Lempp et al., 2019; von Wulffen et al., 2017; Morin et al., 2020), which is sufficiently fast to explain most observations (Figures 1 and 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on transcriptional regulation kinetics and comparison with model predictions.

claim: The immediate decrease in glucose uptake flux in response to a pulse of acetate suggests the existence of additional regulatory mechanisms that act on a faster time scale than transcriptional regulation.
source: However, the immediate decrease in glucose uptake flux in response to a pulse of acetate (Figure 3C) suggests the existence of additional regulatory mechanisms that act on a faster time scale.
evidence: This is an inference from the rapid response observed in Figure 3C.

claim: Additional regulatory mechanisms could operate at the post-transcriptional level, possibly via the carbon storage regulator system or the BarA/UvrY two-component system.
source: These mechanisms could operate at the post-transcriptional level (possibly via the carbon storage regulator system [Revelles et al., 2013] or the BarA/UvrY two-component system [Chavez et al., 2010])
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to relevant regulatory systems.

claim: Additional regulatory mechanisms could operate at the post-translational level, possibly via protein acetylation by acetyl-phosphate.
source: at the post-translational level (possibly via protein acetylation by acetyl-phosphate [Weinert et al., 2013; Ren et al., 2019])
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to studies on protein acetylation.

claim: Additional regulatory mechanisms could operate directly at the metabolic level, possibly via α-ketoglutarate or ATP, which control the glycolytic flux.
source: and/or directly at the metabolic level itself (possibly via α-ketoglutarate [Doucette et al., 2011] or ATP [Koebmann et al., 2002], which control the glycolytic flux).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to studies on metabolic regulation.

claim: The direction of the acetate flux is controlled thermodynamically and is fundamentally determined by the extracellular concentration of acetate.
source: Our results confirm that the direction of the acetate flux is controlled thermodynamically and is fundamentally determined by the extracellular concentration of acetate.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling and experimental results.

claim: Intracellular control of the acetate flux is distributed around the acetyl-CoA node, such that none of the three processes (glycolytic, TCA, and acetate pathways) can be regarded as the sole kinetic bottleneck.
source: Moreover, we found that intracellular control of the acetate flux is distributed around the acetyl-CoA node, i.e., between the glycolytic, TCA, and acetate pathways, such that none of the three processes can be regarded as the sole kinetic bottleneck.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the metabolic control analysis.

claim: The inhibition of the glycolytic and TCA pathways by acetate gives rise to unusual control properties.
source: The inhibition of the glycolytic and TCA pathways by acetate gives rise to unusual control properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the metabolic control analysis comparing different model versions.

claim: The intracellular flux control pattern is determined by the concentration of acetate itself, with a progressive shift of control from the acetate pathway to the rest of the metabolism when the acetate concentration increases.
source: The intracellular flux control pattern is indeed determined by the concentration of acetate itself, with a progressive shift of control from the acetate pathway to the rest of the metabolism when the acetate concentration increases.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the metabolic control analysis.

claim: Metabolic engineering interventions aiming at minimising acetate production should rebalance the flux capacity of both the glycolytic and the TCA pathways, possibly via global metabolic regulators, while accounting for the concentration-dependent effect of acetate on intracellular control patterns.
source: This means that metabolic engineering interventions aiming at minimising acetate production in biotechnology should rebalance the flux capacity of both the glycolytic and the TCA pathways, possibly via global metabolic regulators, while accounting for the concentration-dependent effect of acetate on intracellular control patterns.
evidence: This is a practical implication derived from the control analysis results.

claim: The regulatory scheme involved in E. coli's response to changes in acetate concentration involves direct metabolic regulation of the acetate pathway in combination with indirect regulation of the glycolytic and TCA pathways.
source: We demonstrate that this scheme involves direct metabolic regulation of the acetate pathway in combination with indirect – at least partly transcriptional – regulation of the glycolytic and TCA pathways
evidence: This is a conclusion from the response coefficient analysis and transcriptomic data.

claim: The equal contribution of direct and indirect regulatory mechanisms explains the diverse patterns of acetate flux observed and forms part of E. coli's global physiological response to changing acetate concentrations.
source: and we show how this equal contribution of direct and indirect regulatory mechanisms explains the diverse patterns of acetate flux observed and forms part of E. coli's global physiological response to changing acetate concentrations.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the response coefficient analysis.

claim: The distinct regulatory patterns at high and low acetate concentrations determine the metabolic status of acetate as a co-substrate or by-product of glucose metabolism.
source: The distinct regulatory patterns at high and low acetate concentrations also determine the metabolic status of acetate as a co-substrate or by-product of glucose metabolism.
evidence: This is an inference from the response coefficient analysis showing different regulatory modes.

claim: Acetate should not be considered a terminal, wasteful product of glucose metabolism since it may equally be a co-substrate of glucose.
source: Acetate should not be considered a terminal, wasteful product of glucose metabolism since it may equally be a co-substrate of glucose.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that acetate flux can reverse and acetate can be consumed.

claim: Acetate is a key regulator that induces a global remodelling of E. coli physiology and modulates several cellular functions including motility, biofilm formation, transport, metabolism, and translation.
source: Moreover, it is also a key regulator that induces a global remodelling of E. coli physiology and modulates several cellular functions (motility, biofilm formation, transport, metabolism, translation).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the transcriptomic data showing widespread gene expression changes.

claim: In the intestine, E. coli's environmental niche, the concentration of acetate is high (between 30 and 100 mM).
source: In the intestine however, E. coli's environmental niche, the concentration of acetate is high (between 30 and 100 mM) (Macfarlane et al., 1992; Cummings and Englyst, 1987)
evidence: Supported by citations to studies measuring acetate in the intestine.

claim: Intestinal acetate levels are well above the ~10 mM threshold at which the acetate flux reverses.
source: and well above the ~10 mM threshold at which the acetate flux reverses
evidence: This is an inference comparing intestinal acetate levels to the threshold determined in this study.

claim: High acetate levels in the intestine should favour co-utilisation of acetate with available sugars.
source: These levels of acetate should thus favour its co-utilisation with available sugars
evidence: This is an inference based on the model predictions at high acetate concentrations.

claim: Acetogenic species may be an important source of nutrients for E. coli in the intestine.
source: suggesting that acetogenic species may be an important source of nutrients for E. coli.
evidence: This is speculation based on the inference that E. coli consumes acetate at high concentrations.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae can co-consume ethanol and glucose.
source: Saccharomyces cerevisiae can co-consume ethanol and glucose (Raamsdonk et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citation to Raamsdonk et al., 2001.

claim: Mammalian cells co-assimilate lactate with glucose.
source: and mammalian cells co-assimilate lactate with glucose (Hui et al., 2020; Hui et al., 2017; Rabinowitz and Enerbäck, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hui et al., 2020; Hui et al., 2017; Rabinowitz and Enerbäck, 2020.

claim: Overflow metabolism should be considered a reversible process.
source: These similarities, which have important implications for cell energy and redox balance, indicate that overflow metabolism should be considered a reversible process
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the similarities across different organisms.

claim: There exists a universal phenomenon similar to acetate regulation in E. coli across other organisms.
source: and point to the existence of a universal phenomenon similar to the one described here for acetate in E. coli.
evidence: This is speculation based on the similarities observed across organisms.

claim: E. coli K-12 MG1655 was grown in M9 medium complemented with 15 mM glucose.
source: E. coli K-12 MG1655 was grown in M9 medium (Nicolas et al., 2007) complemented with 15 mM glucose.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions used.

claim: A conversion factor of 0.37 gDW/L/OD unit was used to determine the biomass concentration.
source: and a conversion factor of 0.37 gDW/L/OD unit (Revelles et al., 2013) was used to determine the biomass concentration.
evidence: This describes a methodological parameter supported by citation.

claim: Four independent biological replicates were analysed for each condition in the transcriptomics experiments.
source: Four independent biological replicates were analysed for each condition.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The model contains six reactions, six species, and two compartments (the environment and the cell).
source: The model contains six reactions, six species, and two compartments (the environment and the cell, with a cell volume of 1.77 × 10−3 (L/gDW) Chassagnole et al., 2002; Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the model structure with citation for cell volume parameter.

claim: Growth rates were calculated from the flux of the TCA cycle assuming a constant biomass production yield from acetyl-CoA.
source: Growth rates were calculated from the flux of the TCA cycle assuming a constant biomass production yield from acetyl-CoA, in keeping with observations (Enjalbert et al., 2017; Pinhal et al., 2019).
